profile.name: Diego Espina Rodríguez
profile.headline: .NET backends that hold up *under real load.*
profile.intro: Backend developer specialised in .NET, SQL Server and the Azure ecosystem. I design APIs, integrations and business-critical logic, with asynchronous processing, measured performance and automated deployments straight from the repositories.
profile.bio:
I design APIs from scratch with an isolated data access layer, and I have taken queries and endpoints from tens of seconds down to sub-second responses. I work with automated tests, message queues and business logic that stays consistent even when things fail.

I am at home in the Microsoft Azure and Azure DevOps ecosystem: I set up CI/CD pipelines connected to the repositories to automate testing, builds and deployments. I work with Azure cloud services and storage, including Azure Blob Storage, and keep bringing these workflows into my own projects.

I use Claude, by Anthropic, and Codex, by OpenAI, every day as part of my development work. I keep learning about their models and tools, try out their improvements and look at how to apply them to code. I also install and run AI models and LLMs on my own machines to learn how to manage data, configuration and inference locally.

I like to understand the whole system, including what its users see. That is why I complement the backend with React and TypeScript when a project needs it, and I maintain WordPress sites in production with PHP.
profile.personal: Competitive league footballer and gym every day. The consistency, discipline and teamwork the pitch demands are the same ones I bring to code.

projects.title: ERP Solmicro Expertis
projects.description: Rollout, maintenance and day-to-day improvement of the Expertis ERP (now Solmicro) at client sites, working directly with clients and with the vendor.
projects.details:
It is not my product, but it is one of the pieces where I have had the most impact. During my time at Adico I worked every day on the Expertis ERP, now Solmicro: rolling it out at clients, keeping production installations healthy and improving them continuously.

I built custom developments on top of the ERP for companies with databases of millions of records: calculation engines and business rules for invoicing, inventory and administrative workflows, optimisation of T-SQL queries and procedures, and integrations with external systems.

The work went both ways: direct contact with the client to understand each need and validate what was delivered, and with the ERP vendor to resolve issues and fit the developments into the product.
highlights: ERP rollout at clients and go-live in production
Day-to-day maintenance and improvement of installations with millions of records
Custom developments in C#, VB.NET and T-SQL on top of the ERP
Queries and reports from tens of seconds to under one second
Direct liaison with the client and with the ERP vendor

projects.title: Asynchronous XML catalogue generation
projects.description: Asynchronous process that reads pending jobs and generates the XML product catalogues of an international industrial client.
projects.details:
During my time at Wembley Studios I designed and built an asynchronous process that reads pending jobs and generates from them the XML files of the product catalogues of an international industrial client.

Because it runs in the background, catalogue generation does not block the application while it is being processed.

The project belongs to the client and the company, so here I describe my part at a high level. I am happy to go into more detail in a conversation.
highlights: Design and implementation of the process
Asynchronous execution in the background
XML catalogue generation from the pending jobs

projects.title: Murmur · Meeting transcriber
projects.description: Transcribes meetings with timestamps, tells speakers apart and writes summaries with models that run locally.
projects.details:
A complete application to transcribe meetings without relying on paid AI APIs. You record from the browser or upload an audio or video file, follow the progress live and get a transcript with speakers that you can search, summarise and export.

The backend, in ASP.NET Core on .NET 10, receives files by streaming, queues them in SQL Server and processes them in the background: Whisper.net transcribes, pyannote Community-1 separates the speakers and Ollama writes the summaries. Progress reaches the frontend through Server-Sent Events. The frontend, Murmur, is built with React and TypeScript.
highlights: Persistent queue in SQL Server and background processing
Real-time progress through Server-Sent Events
Diarisation of the whole meeting with stable voice identities
Summaries with decisions, tasks and references to the original segments
Local models: no OpenAI keys and no paid API usage

projects.title: Peluquería Lucía Espina
projects.description: Public website and management for a hair salon, in production: ASP.NET Core 10 and SQL Server on Azure App Service, released with GitHub Actions and Cloudflare.
projects.details:
Website and internal management for the eco-friendly hair salon Peluquería Ecológica Lucía Espina, in production at luciapeluqueriaecologica.com. A single application brings together the salon's public website, in Spanish and English, and a private back office for the daily work: clients and their history, visits and payments, a catalogue with prices, receipts, verified reviews and Excel export.

The public side includes a built-in booking system: it shows availability, takes appointment requests and confirms them through private links that expire. Reviews are verified with the code of a paid receipt and moderated from the dashboard. The back office requires a password and Microsoft Authenticator, with recovery codes, revocable sessions and CSRF protection.

Layered architecture: Domain, Application, Infrastructure and Web. ASP.NET Core MVC with Razor views, Entity Framework Core and SQL Server; independent libraries for email and WhatsApp. The sections below walk through how I took it from the salon's computer to Azure and how each version is released.

sections.title: From the salon's computer to the cloud
sections.text:
The first version ran on the salon's computer, on IIS with a local SQL Server, with the connection string in the Windows credential manager and the keys encrypted with DPAPI. When moving to Azure I did not want to maintain two code bases: the application detects where it runs and takes each piece from the right place. On Windows it keeps using IIS, DPAPI and the credential store; on Azure, the Web App configuration, Key Vault and the managed identity.

That meant isolating behind contracts everything that depended on the environment: where photos are stored, how keys are encrypted, where the email password comes from or which header carries the visitor's real IP.

sections.title: Azure: App Service, Azure SQL and Key Vault
sections.text:
The website runs on Azure App Service for Linux with a B1 plan: a small instance, enough for a salon, with Always On so that the first screen of the day does not wait for the application to start. It only accepts HTTPS, FTP is disabled and the start-up command is the .NET 10 assembly itself.

The database is Azure SQL at the Basic tier (5 DTU), because the free offer is not available in the chosen region, with the Modern_Spanish_CI_AS collation so that searches by name ignore case and accents just like the local SQL Server. Key Vault holds the key with which ASP.NET Core protects its data (Authenticator, appointment links, review codes) and the email secret. Everything lives in Spain Central, in its own resource group, and the cost is around twenty dollars a month.

sections.title: No passwords: managed identity
sections.text:
No part of the system uses passwords. The Web App has a system-assigned managed identity; the SQL server only accepts Microsoft Entra authentication, and the application signs in with that identity: the connection string carries Authentication=Active Directory Managed Identity and no secret. In the database, that identity exists as an external user created with T-SQL, with just the permissions it needs.

Key Vault works the same way, with role-based permissions: the Web App identity only has the role it needs to use the data protection key. The cookie keys are stored in SQL encrypted with that key, so a copy of the database is useless without Key Vault. The SMTP password arrives as a reference to a Key Vault secret, never as a value in the configuration.

sections.title: Releases with GitHub Actions and OIDC
sections.text:
The repository is public and the main branch is protected: it only changes through a pull request, with the build and tests green and the owner's approval. Each pull request starts a temporary SQL Server container in GitHub Actions and runs the domain, security and data migration tests.

When merging into main, the workflow repeats the tests, waits for the manual approval of the production environment, publishes to App Service and checks that the website answers 200. GitHub signs in to Azure with a federated identity (OIDC): Azure trusts the token GitHub issues for that repository and that environment, so the repository secrets hold only identifiers, no credential to steal or rotate.

sections.title: Migrations with real data
sections.text:
The database holds the real data of the business, so the Entity Framework Core migrations are always additive: they add columns and indexes and move data before removing anything, and the previous version keeps working with the new schema. The deployment does not apply them: I apply them before publishing, with my Entra account and my IP in the server firewall, so the new code finds the schema ready.

An automated test rebuilds the previous version's database with data, migrates it and checks that nothing is lost. The catalogue and review photos live in the persistent storage of App Service, which survives every deployment.

sections.title: Domain and DNS with Cloudflare
sections.text:
The domain is on Cloudflare. First I added the domain and its www as custom domains of the Web App and created on Cloudflare the records Azure asks for to validate them (a verification TXT and the name record), with the proxy off until Azure accepted the domain.

Then I generated a long-lived origin certificate on Cloudflare, converted it to PFX and uploaded it to App Service bound to both names through SNI. With that in place I set the TLS mode to Full (strict): the visitor talks to Cloudflare over HTTPS and Cloudflare talks to Azure over HTTPS with a certificate it verifies. Finally I turned on the proxy on the DNS records.

sections.title: Only Cloudflare reaches the origin
sections.text:
With the proxy on, the origin must not accept traffic that does not come from Cloudflare: otherwise anyone who discovers the Web App address would bypass the filter. The App Service access restrictions allow only the IP ranges Cloudflare publishes and deny everything else.

From then on, the visitor's real IP travels in the CF-Connecting-IP header, which the application uses for lockout after failed sign-ins and for per-IP limits. The header is enabled only once the restriction is in place, because without it anyone could forge it. The allowed hosts list closes the rest.

sections.title: What changes and what does not when publishing
sections.text:
Some things work the same in the salon and in the cloud. The thermal receipt printer is driven by the salon's browser over USB with WebUSB: the server only builds the ESC/POS receipt, so printing keeps working with the website published on Azure over HTTPS. The time zone is fixed to Europe/Madrid and the culture to es-ES for dates and amounts.

The ARM templates of the plan and the Web App are in the repository to recreate the environment, and the documentation covers step by step the configuration, the federated identity, the migrations and Cloudflare, so anyone can reproduce the setup.

highlights: In production at luciapeluqueriaecologica.com, in Spanish and English
Clients, visits, payments, receipts, catalogue and Excel export
Built-in booking with availability and confirmation through private links
Back office with MFA, revocable sessions and reviews verified by receipt
Azure App Service Linux B1, Azure SQL Basic and Key Vault in Spain Central
No passwords: managed identity for SQL and Key Vault
GitHub Actions with OIDC federated identity and production approval
Additive migrations applied before publishing and tested with data
Cloudflare: DNS, origin certificate, strict TLS and origin restricted to its IPs
Receipt printer over WebUSB from the salon's browser

projects.title: Subscription Billing Engine

Explicit accounting rounding rules
Unit tests in xUnit over the domain

projects.title: diegoespinarodriguez.com
projects.description: Design, development and release of my portfolio: .NET 10 and React on an Azure Linux VM, with Docker, CI/CD and deployments over SSH.
projects.details:
A personal website can also show how I work: from separation of concerns in the code to delivering and running software in production. Here I bring backend, frontend, infrastructure and automation together in a system that I build and maintain.

I have organised the project into two repositories and two Docker images, deployed on the same Azure virtual machine. Releases connect GitHub Actions, GHCR, SSH and Docker Compose, with checks beforehand, a protected main branch, production approval and recovery of the previous image if a deployment fails.
highlights: Layered architecture and explicit dependency injection
Frontend and backend in separate repositories and images
Ubuntu VM on Azure and a stack coordinated with Docker Compose
Continuous integration on pull requests and automatic release when main is updated
Protected main branch and approval before production deployments
Images identified by commit and deployed by immutable digest
SSH credentials in GitHub secrets and short-lived registry tokens
Shared lock, HTTP checks and recovery of the previous image
Persistent volume for content, images, statistics and errors
Error catalogue, correlation and a private history with messages in Spanish and English

sections.title: End-to-end design and architecture
sections.text:
I have built and deployed this website as a complete project: experience design, frontend, API, persistence and production operations. I keep the frontend and the backend in separate repositories, each with its own Dockerfile, checks and release cycle.

The API uses ASP.NET Core 10 and separates Domain, Application, Infrastructure and API. Program.cs handles start-up; Startup.cs composes services and middleware through explicit extensions. Business rules, validation, repositories and external clients are connected through contracts and dependency injection. The frontend uses React 19, TypeScript and Vite and is served by Nginx.

sections.title: Azure: a Linux VM as the runtime platform
sections.text:
Production is hosted on an Ubuntu virtual machine on Azure, size B2ats_v2 with x86-64 architecture. I prepared the Linux environment to run Docker and Docker Compose and keep the project stack in a dedicated deployment folder.

The API, web and Cloudflare Tunnel containers live on the same VM. Frontend and backend are two independent images, coordinated by Compose and a shared Docker network. This lets me update one service without rebuilding the other and keep the data between versions.

sections.title: Containers and persistence
sections.text:
The backend Dockerfile builds and publishes the API in a build stage with the .NET 10 SDK. The final image uses the ASP.NET Core runtime on Alpine and runs the application as an unprivileged user. On the frontend, another multi-stage build produces the React files and hands them to Nginx.

The api and web services run with a read-only file system, no additional Linux capabilities and no-new-privileges. Internal traffic goes through diego-portfolio-net. The diego-portfolio-data volume keeps the portfolio content, uploaded images, statistics and error history: these files are not packaged into the images and are not replaced when code is released.

sections.title: Domain and access through Cloudflare Tunnel
sections.text:
Cloudflare manages diegoespinarodriguez.com and its www variant. The cloudflared container opens the outbound tunnel and routes traffic to web:8080 inside the Docker network. Nginx serves React and forwards API requests to the api service.

On the server, the website is only published on the VM's loopback; public visits arrive through the tunnel. SSH is used for administration and releases. The tunnel token stays in the server's private configuration. Proxy headers make it possible to identify the client for rate limiting and to feed the aggregated statistics.

sections.title: One continuous integration process per repository
sections.text:
Each repository contains its own GitHub Actions workflow. Pull requests targeting main run the checks before merging. A change merged into main automatically starts the same validation and, if it passes, builds and publishes the image. There is also a manual run for controlled operations.

On the backend, dependencies are restored, .NET is built and unit tests and integration tests run against a real API with isolated data. On the frontend, dependencies are installed with npm ci and TypeScript and the Vite build are verified. Both workflows check the deployment scripts and their recovery scenarios. External actions are pinned to specific commits to control which version runs.

sections.title: Protected main and production approval
sections.text:
I work on develop and bring changes into main through pull requests. GitHub rules require the repository checks before merging and block direct pushes, deleting main and rewriting its history. A local hook adds a confirmation before each push and rejects direct pushes to main.

After the merge, the pipeline publishes the artefact, but the deployment job waits for my approval in the production environment. The environment restricts releases to main and requires a reviewer, without letting administrators bypass the protection. Before deploying, a script checks that the approval is configured and that the approved commit is still the current main. They are two separate decisions: integrating the change and authorising it into production.

sections.title: Traceable images in GitHub Container Registry
sections.text:
Images are built for linux/amd64 and published to GitHub Container Registry, one for api and one for web. Each version carries the commit SHA and labels that identify its repository and revision.

The deployment pulls the image by its immutable SHA-256 digest. That way the VM runs the artefact built for that commit, and it is possible to tell which version has reached production. The local Compose tag is updated after pulling the digest; nothing is built on the server and no branch that could change during the deployment is pulled.

sections.title: Releases over SSH and credential management
sections.text:
The release connection uses a dedicated SSH key and strict host key verification. The host, user, private key and known_hosts are stored as secrets of the GitHub production environment; their values are not part of the repository. The matching public key is authorised on the VM.

GitHub Actions provides a short-lived GITHUB_TOKEN with write access to packages for publishing and read access for deploying. The pull on the VM receives the token through SSH standard input and docker login uses password-stdin. The runner's and Docker's temporary credentials are removed at the end. The tunnel token and the server's private configuration are kept separately.

sections.title: Deployment, checks and recovery
sections.text:
Both repositories acquire the same lock on the VM so that their deployments never change the stack at the same time. The script validates the service, repository, commit and image reference before continuing. It keeps the previous image and recreates only api or web with Docker Compose, leaving the volumes and the rest of the stack untouched.

It then waits for the container to be healthy and checks both /healthz and /api/health through Nginx. If the update fails after the image has been switched, it tries to restore the previous version, recreates the service and repeats the checks. The run is marked as failed so it can be reviewed. Every completed deployment records the commit, digest, date and the reference of the previous image.

sections.title: Content, observability and maintenance
sections.text:
Professional content is managed from an editor that is only available in Development and from the local machine. The API validates the data and uses a revision to detect concurrent edits; ETag allows reads to be revalidated. The GitHub integration includes caching and a degraded result when the external service does not respond.

Portfolio.Errors centralises error codes and messages. The API returns structured error responses with HTTP status, language and correlation; the private history is persisted in the volume and read from the protected editor. Content and operation and error messages are available in Spanish and English through language.

I keep code releases separate from content maintenance. The volume is preserved when images are updated and has its own backup process. Before replacing data on the server I prepare a backup and review the operation. The JSON persistence is designed for a single instance; moving to several replicas would mean taking those contracts to a database and shared storage.

experience.summary: Backend in C# and .NET 8 on business domains with dense rules, from design to production support.
highlights: Asynchronous process generating XML product catalogues for an international industrial client.
Design and implementation from scratch of more than 25 REST endpoints with chained validations, state machines and edge cases solved without breaking contracts already in production.

Integrations with third-party systems and APIs through message queues, retries and idempotency, so that processes were repeatable and consistent in the face of failures, timeouts or partial responses.
Unit and integration tests on the business logic and critical endpoints, run in the pipeline on every delivery.
Full cycle on Azure and Azure DevOps: CI/CD pipelines, deployments to QA and production, and diagnosis of production incidents.
Internal R&D project: an AI-based agent to automate recurring queries and tasks on Azure DevOps.

entries.title: Compromised intermediate certificates: how I upgraded the Cloudflare Tunnel
entries.text:
Cloudflare published a security advisory: eight eMudhra intermediate certificates had weak private keys. With them, anyone can issue valid certificates for any domain and impersonate legitimate websites. cloudflared, the Cloudflare Tunnel connector, trusted those certificates in versions before 2026.10.2, and Cloudflare recommended upgrading every instance. According to the advisory itself, there was no evidence of active exploitation.

On this website the tunnel is the only way in for public traffic: the Azure virtual machine exposes no ports to the Internet for visitors and everything arrives through it. A connector that trusts a compromised certificate authority sits exactly at the most sensitive point, so I treated it as a priority.

cloudflared runs as a container in the docker compose, with a pinned version and no automatic updates. That is a deliberate choice: reproducible deployments and no change I have not reviewed first. The trade-off is that upgrading it is on me, because the GitHub Actions pipeline only deploys the API and the frontend.

I made the change by hand through the server's administrative access: I moved the image to the fixed version and recreated only the tunnel container, leaving the API and the frontend untouched. The website stopped answering for a few seconds. The same change is versioned in the repository, so the compose file on the server and the one in the code do not drift apart.

The scope was limited: the tunnel hands traffic to the frontend over HTTP inside the internal Docker network, so origin certificates were not involved and the TLS configuration did not need to change.

My takeaway: pinning versions is still the right call, but it turns every pinned dependency into a commitment. You have to follow its security advisories and know how to upgrade it when it sits outside the usual pipeline.

entries.title: Why my website has its own backend
entries.text:
A personal website could be a static HTML page. I preferred to treat it as one more project, with the same decisions I would make in a real product.

The API is split into Domain, Application, Infrastructure and API. Controllers only translate HTTP; the rules live in services and persistence in repositories. Content is stored with a revision number, so two simultaneous edits never overwrite each other, and that same revision works as an ETag so the browser does not download what it already has.

The GitHub section queries the public API with an in-memory cache. If GitHub fails or rate-limits the requests, the last valid result is served and there is no retry loop. The frontend and the API live in separate repositories and containers, without a root user and with a read-only file system.

entries.title: What I bring from the pitch to code
entries.text:
I play competitive league football and train at the gym every day. Away from the screen there is method too.

From the pitch I take the consistency of repeating the basics well, the discipline of preparing before it is needed and the idea that the team matters more than the individual play. In code that means tests before deploying, measuring before optimising and leaving work that is easy to understand for whoever comes next.
